Testing the Test: calibrating α

Maisie Mary Cu · Berlin School of Economics and Law

The significance threshold is a decision rule. This simulator finds the α that minimises expected loss for a stated sample size, effect size, prevalence of true effects and cost ratio, checks it against study-level replication evidence, and tests how well it survives wrong inputs and researchers who react to it. Every result is computed two ways: by the model (the formulas) and by simulation (generating studies one by one), shown side by side so you can see they agree.

What this study is about

The question

Almost every empirical field decides whether a result is "real" by checking whether its p-value is below 0.05. That cut-off is the same for a pilot study of twenty people and a registry of two hundred thousand, for a screen where almost nothing is true and a confirmatory trial where most things are, and for decisions whose mistakes cost very different amounts.

How should the significance threshold be set when false positives and false negatives have different probabilities and different consequences, and does a threshold set that way do better than the fixed conventions of .05 and .005?

The idea in one paragraph

A significance test is a decision rule, and every decision rule makes two kinds of mistake. This study treats the threshold α as something to calculate rather than assume: it is the value that minimises the expected cost of both mistakes, given the sample size, the size of the effect worth detecting, how often tested ideas are true, and how much worse a false positive is than a missed discovery. The simulator on this page is that calculation, built as a working engine, checked against simulated studies, and applied to replication data and to industry settings.

What is new

  • A general mapping from a stated decision environment to a recommended threshold, with its power, error rates and expected loss.
  • The cost ratio that the .05 convention implicitly assumes, measured from replication data, and a ceiling on it: at balanced prevalence .05 cannot be optimal if a false positive costs more than about 3.4 missed discoveries.
  • A working engine, validated by simulation, that turns "justify your alpha" into a procedure.

How it is done

  • Expected-loss minimisation over the two error types (statistical decision theory).
  • Exact power for the two-sample t-test, with a closed-form approximation that explains the results.
  • Monte Carlo validation: 200,000 simulated studies per environment in the paper; live simulations on this page.
  • Study-level analysis of 94 replications from the Reproducibility Project: Psychology.

Data used

  • Reproducibility Project: Psychology (Open Science Collaboration, 2015), study-level file.
  • FORRT Replication Database and the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (Appendix A of the paper).
  • SECOM semiconductor manufacturing data (UCI repository) for an industrial application (Appendix B).

Start here Statistics in 5 minutes: what this simulator is for, in plain language

The problem

Scientists, doctors, engineers and companies constantly have to decide whether something is real or just luck: does a new drug work, is this wafer faulty, did the new website design help? Data is noisy, so any decision rule makes two kinds of mistake:

  • False alarm (false positive): saying something works when it doesn't.
  • Missed discovery (false negative): saying nothing is there when something is.

An everyday picture: a smoke alarm

Make a smoke alarm very sensitive and it goes off every time you make toast. Make it dull and it sleeps through a real fire. The right setting depends on how often fires actually happen and how bad each mistake is. A kitchen and a fireworks warehouse should not have the same setting.

The p-value and ".05"

A p-value is a surprise score: how unusual the data would be if nothing were going on. Small means surprising. Researchers declare a finding "significant" when the p-value is below a cut-off, almost always 0.05, in every field and every situation. That is like setting every smoke alarm in the world to the same sensitivity.

What this machine does

You describe the situation with four dials, and the machine finds the cut-off that makes the fewest costly mistakes on average (called α*):

  • n: how much data each study collects.
  • δ: how big a real effect would be.
  • π: how often the ideas being tested are actually true.
  • C: how many missed discoveries one false alarm is worth.

Model and simulation

The model works the answer out with formulas, like calculating the odds in a dice game. The simulation plays the situation out thousands of times on the computer and counts what actually happens, like rolling the dice for real. When the two agree (a green ✓), the formulas can be trusted.

What it finds

The best cut-off changes enormously with the situation, from about 0.0003 for gene hunting to 0.5 for medical triage. 0.05 is only right in a narrow band of situations. Using it everywhere quietly assumes a fixed view of how bad a false alarm is compared with a miss, and that view is rarely stated or checked.

Words you will see

Power
The chance a study catches a real effect when there is one.
Prevalence (π)
The share of tested ideas that are actually true.
Cost ratio (C)
How much worse a false alarm is than a missed discovery. C = 2 means one false alarm hurts as much as two misses.
Expected loss
The average cost of mistakes per study if you used this rule forever.
α* (alpha star)
The cut-off with the lowest expected loss.
Regret
How much worse a choice is than the best possible one.
SE (standard error)
How much a simulated number would wobble if you ran it again. "Within 2 SE" means the difference is just luck.

How it works: the engine, built from the bottom up

The study is built in layers. Each layer takes the output of the one below and adds one idea. The gauges show each part's reading at the current engine settings and at your dragged threshold, so you can change a setting in tab 1 and watch every layer respond.

Reference

Decision problem

L(α) = (1 − π)·C·α + π·β(α; δ, n) α* = argmin L(α), α ∈ [.0001, .50] power: two-sided two-sample t, ν = 2n − 2, λ = δ·√(n/2) F(t) ≈ Φ( (t·(1 − 1/(4ν)) − λ) / √(1 + t²/(2ν)) ), 1 − β = 1 − F(t_crit) + F(−t_crit)

Closed-form approximation (normal power)

z* = λ/2 + ln(2(1 − π)C/π)/λ α* ≈ 2[1 − Φ(z*)] C at which .05 is optimal ≈ π/(2(1 − π)) · exp(1.96λ − λ²/2) ceiling over all designs (λ = 1.96): C ≤ 3.41 · π/(1 − π)

Replication evidence

z_i = atanh(r_rep,i) ~ (1 − w)·N(0, s_i²) + w·N(μ, τ² + s_i²), s_i = 1/√(N_i − 3) w = PPV (share true among published significant findings) π = PPV·α₀ / ( P·(1 − PPV) + PPV·α₀ ), P = mean power of the original studies

Robustness and feedback

regret R(α; θ) = L(α; θ) − min_a L(a; θ) uncertainty-aware α = argmin_α mean over draws of L(α; θ̂ + noise) π(α) = E[ q | q·(1 − β(hα)) + (1 − q)·hα ≥ b ], equilibrium: α = α*(π(α))

Data and caveats

  • RPP study-level file: RPPdataConverted (Open Science Collaboration, 2015; github.com/CenterForOpenScience/rpp). Reproduces 35 of 97 replicated overall, 7 of 31 for JPSP and 13 of 27 for JEP:LMC.
  • Replication effects are modelled on Fisher's z scale with a normal approximation; the engine presets use half the median original N as n per group.
  • JPSP and JEP:LMC alone have about 27 studies each and are not identified: their implied-C intervals are unbounded. The discipline groups pool all three journals.
  • Converting PPV to π assumes the original studies' false-positive rate. Tab 2 shows the effect of .10 and .20 to allow for analytic flexibility.
  • The live run draws each t statistic exactly as (Z + λ) / √(χ²/ν), with λ = δ√(n/2) for a true effect and 0 for a null, so it does not rely on the power approximation.
  • Industry cases marked "Illustrative" (finance, A/B testing, Phase III) use assumed inputs, not estimates; replace them with your own before citing. The semiconductor case uses the one-sided test of Appendix B.
  • "P(real | a result like this)" in the p-value explorer is computed from the t distribution over |t| within ±0.15 of the dragged value, the same window the simulation check counts.
  • The robustness and feedback tabs are simulations under stated assumptions, not estimates.

ModelSimulation Wrong inputs: how much does calibration lose?

The true environment is whatever is set in the engine (chapter 2). Each simulated analyst sees π and C with noise of size σ (on the logit and log scales) and picks a threshold. Regret is the extra expected loss over the best possible threshold. This tests hypotheses H1 to H3.

The model column computes each analyst's regret from the formula. The live simulation then makes each analyst actually run studies with the threshold they chose, and measures the regret that really happens.

Each dot is one analystMean95th percentile

Pilot grid result (96 environments, 40 analysts each)

Model Researchers react to the threshold

Candidate hypotheses vary in how plausible they are. A researcher runs a study only if the chance of a significant result clears a publication bar, so the threshold changes which hypotheses get tested and therefore π. The equilibrium is where the engine's α*(π) and the researchers' π(α) agree. Uses n, δ and C from the engine in chapter 2.

Evidence and results

What replication data says, every table in one place, and maps of the whole study.

Model Replication evidence: Reproducibility Project: Psychology

Study-level estimates from 94 originally significant findings with a completed replication (Open Science Collaboration, 2015). A two-groups mixture separates true effects from nulls in the replication results. The share of true effects among published significant findings (PPV) is then converted into the share among tested hypotheses (π), which is the input the engine needs.

Cost ratio at which .05 is optimal

Log scale, 90% bootstrap interval. Below 1 means .05 is only right if missing an effect is worse than a false claim. Hollow markers show the current draft's values.

Share of true effects: published vs tested

The draft's π is a PPV. The prior π the engine needs is much lower wherever original power is high.

Part IV

Findings and assumptions

What it all means, and what it rests on.

Findings

From the headline to the detail. Numbers in blue are calculated live on this page.

Assumptions and inputs

Every number the engine depends on, where it comes from, why it was chosen, and the range tested.

Assumptions register

Conventions

  • The cost of a missed discovery is fixed at 1; C is the cost of a false positive in those units. Only the ratio matters.
  • Expected loss is per study, averaged over true and null hypotheses in proportion to π.
  • Thresholds are searched between .0001 and .50; results at either end are marked as boundary solutions.
  • "Agree" means the simulated value is within 2.5 standard errors of the model value.

Limits of the model

  • One test family: the two-sample t-test with equal groups (plus one-sided z for the semiconductor case).
  • Loss counts errors, not how wrong an estimate is (no type S or type M costs yet).
  • Prevalence and effect size from replication data are literature averages, not the values facing a single study.
  • The cost ratio is a judgement. The questionnaire in chapter 2 helps state it but does not estimate it.
  • Fixed sample size: no sequential or anytime-valid testing.
